lesson_title: How Old Is the Fleet, Really? Fixed Assets and the Auditors
hook_text: Two numbers on a balance sheet can tell you the machines are seven years old — and that the business has three years to act.
clip_script: Your aunt owns delivery taxis, and her equipment story hides in two numbers anyone can read. The equipment cost nine hundred thousand rand, and she writes off ninety thousand a year — machines like this last about ten years. The wear account has gathered six hundred and thirty thousand. Now divide: six thirty gathered, at ninety a year — the equipment is SEVEN years old. Ten-year life, seven consumed. Three years left. And three years is not a bookkeeping fact — it is a countdown. A business that waits until year ten meets the replacement bill broke. So the smart owner starts now: a fund, finance, one machine replaced at a time. Then the fleet-wide health check, one comparison: what she ADDED this year against what the year WORE. Added four hundred thousand, wore two thirty — the fleet is getting younger. Flip those numbers year after year and a business is quietly eating itself — and here is the cruel part: the eating years LOOK profitable, because so little is being spent. Plenty of businesses have flattered themselves straight into a dead fleet. Two balance-sheet numbers, one division, one comparison — and you can read any company's future maintenance bill before its own directors admit it.
visual_style: A taxi depot at dawn; odometer-style counters rolling to show cost and accumulated wear, a big division landing on the number seven; a countdown clock over the fleet, then a split-screen of a renewing fleet against a rusting one.
pacing: Two-number setup, satisfying division beat, countdown tension, hard flip to the warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any fixed asset note like a fleet inspector.
